setupSteps: Pick your area and check the floor. Use a flat, non-slip area clear of bags, dumbbells and people. Confirm what your gym allows: many Indian gyms do not allow dropping weights, so plan to lower the bar under control every rep.

Choose the bar and plates. An Olympic men's bar is usually 20 kg and 2.2 m long (est.; check the label, women's bars and some gym bars differ). Standard bumper plates are 450 mm across at every weight; iron plates shrink as the weight falls, so a light iron plate puts the bar lower than a heavy one and makes the start harder (Bells of Steel; Liftbigeatbig). Beginners often feel the pull is easier and safer from the standard height. If the plates are small, raise the bar to the standard height on blocks, or set it in a rack or on safety pins at that height (Starting Strength advice).

Load evenly. Same plates on both sides, pushed fully on, with the bar level when you look from the end. Fit the collars or clips on both sides, even for light sets. Plates sliding on one side can tip the bar.
Start with the empty bar or light plates. The empty bar (20 kg, est.) is enough for the first sessions while you learn the position. Build up slowly (Gym 4).
Shoes. Flat, firm-soled shoes or bare feet where allowed. Thick cushioned running shoes make you less stable. No sliders or sandals.
Belt (optional). A lifting belt is not needed for light technique work. See the belt note under Safety.

Stand with the bar over your mid-foot. Feet about hip-width apart (about the width of your pelvis, est.), toes straight or turned out slightly. The bar should be over the middle of your foot, about over the shoelaces, about an inch from your shins (Starting Strength). If you look down, you should not see the laces' knot hiding under the bar (coaching advice).
Hinge and grip. Push your hips back and bend down while keeping the back flat, until you can reach the bar. Your hands should be just outside your legs, so your arms hang straight down.
Double overhand (both palms toward you). The starting grip for beginners and for lighter sets. It keeps the shoulders even (coaching sources).

Hook grip. Same overhand grip, but the thumbs go under the fingers. It can let you hold heavier loads and is common in Olympic lifting; it can hurt the thumbs at first (coaching sources). Learn it after double overhand.

Mixed grip (one palm toward you, one away). Most common in powerlifting for heavy sets because it stops the bar rolling. The downside is that the arm with the palm turned away (supinated) is placed so its biceps tendon is more exposed to strain, and the shoulders get uneven (coaching sources). Switch your hands from set to set if you use it, and use only after the double overhand grip is the limit.
Straps are an extra tool, used after your grip runs out on heavier sets; do not use them to hide poor grip on every set.
Drop the hips only as far as needed. Bend your knees until your shins touch the bar. Do not drop the hips lower or the shins will push the bar ahead of your mid-foot (Starting Strength).
Chest up, neck neutral. Look at a spot on the floor about 2 m in front (est.).
Engage the lats. Imagine squeezing oranges in your armpits or bending the bar around your shins. Your lats hold the bar close and your arms stay straight (Starting Strength; coaching sources).
Brace. Take a breath into your belly and tighten your stomach as if bracing for a light punch, before the bar leaves the floor.

steps.title: Walk up to the bar
steps.action: Stand with the bar over your mid-foot, feet hip-width apart.
steps.feel: Weight spread across the whole foot.
steps.visualCheck: Side: bar over the middle of the foot. Front: feet even, toes straight or slightly out.

steps.title: Hinge and grip the bar
steps.action: Push your hips back and bend down with a flat back, then grab the bar just outside your legs.
steps.feel: Stretch in the back of the thighs; weight stays in the whole foot, not on the toes.
steps.breathing: Breathe out gently as you go down.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back flat, not rounded; arms straight and hanging under the shoulders. Front: hands even and just outside the legs.

steps.title: Bring the shins to the bar
steps.action: Bend the knees until the shins touch the bar. Do not move the bar.
steps.feel: Shins touch the bar lightly; hamstrings stretched.
steps.visualCheck: Side: shins slightly forward, shoulders slightly in front of the bar, bar still over mid-foot. Front: knees tracking out over the toes.

steps.title: Chest up and lats on
steps.action: Lift your chest, pull your shoulder blades gently down, and squeeze the bar into your legs with your lats.
steps.feel: Tension under the armpits and across the upper back; slack taken out of the bar.
steps.breathing: Breathe in as you take up the slack.
steps.visualCheck: Side: spine neutral from head to tailbone; arms straight. Front: shoulders even, not shrugged.

steps.title: Brace
steps.action: Fill your belly with air and tighten your midsection before you pull.
steps.feel: A firm, wide trunk; lower back not arched hard.
steps.breathing: Hold the breath briefly (a short brace) or take a deep breath and keep tension.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ribs stacked over the hips, not flared; back still flat.

steps.title: Push the floor away
steps.action: Push your feet into the floor and straighten the knees and hips together so the bar rises straight up.
steps.feel: Legs pushing; bar brushing the shins; back staying in position.
steps.breathing: Keep the brace; start breathing out slowly as the bar passes the knees.
steps.visualCheck: Side: bar travels in a straight vertical line close to the legs; hips and shoulders rise together. Front: knees out, not caving.

steps.title: Pass the knees and finish
steps.action: As the bar passes the knees, push the hips forward, squeeze the buttocks and stand tall.
steps.feel: Buttocks squeezing; back long and steady, not bent backwards.
steps.visualCheck: Side: standing straight, shoulders over the hips, ribs down, no backward lean. Front: hips and shoulders level, bar resting on the thighs.

steps.title: Pause briefly at the top
steps.action: Stand tall for a moment with the bar against your thighs.
steps.feel: Tall and steady; knees straight but not forced back.
steps.visualCheck: Side: head, shoulders, hips in one line.

steps.title: Lower the bar
steps.action: Push the hips back first, keeping the bar against the thighs, and bend the knees only once the bar passes them.
steps.feel: Hamstrings stretching; bar sliding down the thighs.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back flat; bar close to the legs in a straight line. Front: knees tracking out.

steps.title: Set it down under control
steps.action: Place the plates on the floor; do not drop them. Let go only when the plates are resting.
steps.breathing: Reset the breath before the next rep.
steps.visualCheck: Bar rests on the floor; plates even.

steps.title: Repeat or finish the set
steps.action: Reset the setup (steps 2-5) for each rep when the bar rests on the floor. After the last rep, stand and step back, then unload the bar.
steps.feel: Legs and back tired but steady; no sharp pain.
steps.visualCheck: Bar rests flat; plates and collars even.

commonMistakes.title: Rounding the lower back
commonMistakes.text: Rounding the lower back. Why: the most common beginner error and it adds disc stress when loaded. Fix: lower the weight, brace, hinge from the hips and stop the set when the back starts to round.

commonMistakes.title: Bar too far from the legs, or drifting forward
commonMistakes.text: Bar too far from the legs, or drifting forward. Why: lengthens the lever on the lower back, so the lift gets harder and riskier. Fix: bar over mid-foot, lats on, bar brushes the shins and thighs.

commonMistakes.title: Hips too low at the start ("squatting the deadlift")
commonMistakes.text: Hips too low at the start ("squatting the deadlift"). Why: shins push the bar forward of mid-foot (Starting Strength). Fix: keep hips higher; set the shins against the bar and stop there.

commonMistakes.title: Hips rising before the shoulders
commonMistakes.text: Hips rising before the shoulders. Why: turns it into a stiff-leg "good-morning" pull and puts the stress on the low back. Fix: lighter weight, push the floor away, keep the chest up as the bar leaves the floor.

commonMistakes.title: Jerking the bar off the floor
commonMistakes.text: Jerking the bar off the floor. Why: yanks the back and loses tension. Fix: take the slack out of the bar first, then push the floor away smoothly.

commonMistakes.title: Hyperextending at the top
commonMistakes.text: Hyperextending at the top. Why: leaning back past upright squeezes the lower back, not the glutes. Fix: stand tall, squeeze the glutes, ribs down.

commonMistakes.title: Dropping the bar after the lift
commonMistakes.text: Dropping the bar after the lift. Why: damages the floor, plates and bar, and is banned in most Indian gyms outside a platform. Fix: lower it with control. Bumper plates are made to be dropped from a platform; iron plates are not (Verve Fitness; Catalyst Athletics).

commonMistakes.title: Looking up into the mirror
commonMistakes.text: Looking up into the mirror. Why: bends the neck back and spoils the line. Fix: pick a spot on the floor.

commonMistakes.title: Going too heavy too soon
commonMistakes.text: Going too heavy too soon. Why: form fails first and the bar rounds the back. Fix: build up slowly with the double progression in Gym 3 and Gym 4.

commonMistakes.title: Turning it into a pull with the arms
commonMistakes.text: Turning it into a pull with the arms. Why: bent elbows cost you tension and can strain the biceps, especially with a mixed grip. Fix: arms straight, lats tight.

safetyNotes: Lower back pain or a past disc problem: the deadlift loads the back directly. Evidence on deadlifts for low back pain is mixed (one trial found benefit for some people with recurrent pain; a pilot found none). Get advice first, use light loads or a regression (rack pull, trap bar, RDL with dumbbells), and stop if pain spreads down the leg or gets worse.

Uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke history, aneurysm: heavy lifting with straining can spike blood pressure (MacDougall et al. 1985). Breathe out on the effort, avoid sets to failure, and get clearance. Do not lift if resting BP is 180/120 mmHg or higher; get clearance at 140-179/90-119 (secondary ACSM-aligned sources).

Osteoporosis, especially with a spine fracture: supervised programmes like LIFTMOR used deadlifts, but they were done under qualified supervision with progressive loading; see a doctor or physiotherapist before starting.

Pregnancy: ACOG's own text on heavy deadlifts was not reached; a 2025 BJSM study in experienced lifters found fetal heart rate did not change after sets at 70-90% of 10-rep max, even with Valsalva, but it excluded beginners. Ask your obstetrician.
Hernia, recent abdominal or pelvic surgery, diastasis recti: straining and bracing raise abdominal pressure; follow your surgeon's limits.
Wrist, elbow or shoulder injuries: heavy gripping and the hanging load can aggravate them; use lighter weight or the trap bar.
Tall or short users: if you cannot reach the bar with a flat back, raise the bar on blocks or plates.

Bumper plates (rubber, 450 mm at every weight, made to be dropped from a platform) vs iron plates (thinner, smaller at light weights, not made to be dropped). Bumpers keep the bar at the same height at every load; light iron plates leave the bar lower, so raise the bar to standard height with blocks or a rack when you use small plates.

Do not drop the bar on a floor or platform that forbids it; lower every rep under control. Never drop an empty bar on a platform, never drop loaded plates on gym equipment or racks, and let a loaded bar land only once and level on bumper plates if your gym allows platform drops (Catalyst Athletics; Youfit; Rep Fitness; GVSU rules).
Use collars on both sides, strip the bar after use, and return plates to the rack.
Keep clear of other people's lanes; do not film strangers; ask before using chalk.
